These sources are FICTIONAL — example.org/example.com domains, invented figures — authored alongside the sample deck so the demo has known-correct answers. They are not market research and must never be cited as such. The same file drives the demo in every format.

sources.title: Workflow automation category sizing, independent composite 2026
sources.snippet: Independent 2026 estimates put the whole workflow-automation category at $18-24B, not the $45-50B figures circulating in vendor-sponsored reports. The larger numbers are 2030 projections that roll legacy RPA seats, iPaaS spend and agent platforms into a single total. The slice a mid-market agentic tool can realistically serve is estimated at $3-5B today. Category growth is 16-19% annually; the 23%+ CAGR sometimes quoted is drawn from the RPA sub-segment during its 2019-2022 peak and has not been observed since.

sources.title: Microsoft bundles Power Automate agent flows into E5 at no incremental cost
sources.snippet: Microsoft now includes Power Automate agent flows in E5 licensing at no incremental per-seat cost. For a mid-market finance or operations team already paying for E5, the marginal cost of adopting the bundled option is effectively zero. Buyers surveyed described their evaluation as 'what does this do that Power Automate cannot' rather than a greenfield purchase. Two of the eleven vendors tracked in this segment repositioned away from general workflow automation during 2026 following the change.

sources.title: Mid-market automation pricing and contract value benchmarks
sources.snippet: Median annual contract value for mid-market workflow automation tooling sits at $19,000, with an interquartile range of $12,000-$31,000. Platform fees between $1,500 and $2,500 per month are common at the upper end, though most vendors at that price point bundle implementation services. An ACV of $28,000 is achievable but sits in the top quartile and generally requires either a multi-department deployment or a services component that carries materially lower margin than the software itself.

sources.title: Inference cost as a share of COGS for LLM-backed products
sources.snippet: Products that run an LLM planner on every workflow execution report gross margins of 55-68% once inference is loaded into COGS, against 78-85% for the same products when inference is reported below the line or absorbed into R&D. The gap widens with execution volume, because inference scales with usage while the rest of the cost base does not. Buyers and investors increasingly ask vendors to state explicitly whether inference sits inside the reported gross margin.

sources.title: Seed-stage B2B SaaS growth and retention benchmarks, 2026 cohort
sources.snippet: Median growth for seed-stage B2B SaaS at $250k-500k ARR is 9-12% month over month; the top quartile runs 15-20%. Sustained 18% monthly growth over four months is therefore above median and genuinely notable at this stage. The benchmark that separates durable from transient growth at this size is net revenue retention on the first cohort, which the median company does not disclose until Series A and which correlates far better with 24-month outcomes than headline growth does.

sources.title: Where mid-market operations budgets actually come from
sources.snippet: Mid-market operations automation is overwhelmingly a substitution purchase rather than net-new budget. In a survey of 240 mid-market operations leaders, 71% funded automation tooling by displacing an existing line item — typically an incumbent iPaaS contract or contractor hours — rather than from incremental budget. This matters for market sizing: a total addressable figure built by counting companies and multiplying by a target contract value will overstate the reachable market, because the buyer must first decide to stop paying someone else.
